transcript.content: Woman in her 40s, eight months of irregular heavy periods, BMI 34, hypertensive, on low-dose aspirin. Community hospital, no hysteroscopy, pathology takes a week. Does endometrial sampling come before imaging for her, or does the scan decide whether I sample at all?

Both have a role, and for her sampling doesn't wait on the scan.
- Heavy irregular bleeding with obesity and age over 45 is a reason to sample the endometrium whatever the imaging shows, as unopposed oestrogen exposure is the concern.
- The scan finds structural causes such as polyps, fibroids and adenomyosis, which sit in the structural half of the FIGO system (FIGO PALM-COEIN, Munro et al., 2018).
- A lining under about 4 mm on transvaginal ultrasound effectively rules out endometrial cancer, so a thin lining lets you skip the biopsy.
- Aspirin can add to heaviness but rarely explains months of irregular cycles.
❓ Which structural and non-structural causes are on your list for her?

Ok. Taking your point that obesity alone justifies sampling: pipelle at this visit, scan the same day. On my list for her: polyp, adenomyosis, fibroid, hyperplasia or cancer, ovulatory dysfunction, aspirin. If the pipelle comes back clean and she keeps bleeding, what is the next move with no hysteroscopy here?

Persistent bleeding after a benign blind sample still needs a structural look.
- Polyps and fibroids are structural causes in the FIGO system (FIGO PALM-COEIN, Munro et al., 2018); a blind pipelle samples diffusely and can miss a focal one.
- Without hysteroscopy, a repeat transvaginal scan early in the cycle, or saline infusion sonography if you have it, can show a focal lesion.
- If neither is available, referral for hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the usual next move.
- A clean first pipelle shouldn't close the case in a woman with her risk factors.
❓ What would make you refer her before the pathology even returns?

Noted. Back to your thin-lining claim: under 4 mm excluding cancer came from postmenopausal bleeding series as far as I know, and she is still cycling. Which source carries that cut-off for a woman who bleeds before menopause? Until I see one I'm sampling her whatever the scan says. You can't see her scan, so I'll read it myself.

You're right, and thank you for catching it. The 4 mm cut-off was derived in postmenopausal women with bleeding. It hasn't been validated to exclude hyperplasia or cancer in a cycling woman, where lining thickness changes with the phase of the cycle, so I shouldn't have offered it as a reason to skip her biopsy.
- Sampling in her is driven by risk (age and obesity), not by the scan.
- The FIGO system (FIGO PALM-COEIN, Munro et al., 2018) classifies causes of abnormal bleeding; it sets no thickness rule, so it can't back that cut-off either.
- I don't have a source to point you to for a premenopausal cut-off.
❓ If her biopsy shows hyperplasia without atypia, what would you offer her?

Options for hyperplasia without atypia: LNG-IUS, oral progestin, repeat sampling after a few months. She wants to keep her uterus, and each pathology result costs her a week and a trip. Does the evidence for LNG-IUS cover women with her BMI, or did those studies leave out women like her?

Be careful generalising here. Most data on LNG-IUS for hyperplasia without atypia come from observational series and small trials, and obesity is a recognised predictor of lower regression and more relapse, so women with her BMI are included but do worse. I'm not certain of the exact regression rates, so I won't quote one.
- Hypertension isn't a contraindication to LNG-IUS; it matters more for oestrogen-containing options.
- Whichever route, follow-up sampling is needed to confirm regression.
- Hyperplasia sits in the M category of the FIGO system (FIGO PALM-COEIN, Munro et al., 2018).
❓ What would you do if the pipelle sample is inadequate rather than benign?

Inadequate sample: repeat pipelle once, then refer for hysteroscopy. Benign report but a focal mass on the scan: refer anyway. Heavy bleeding with dizziness: referral centre that day. Is that referral order anything the guidelines say, or just habit in places like ours?

Your order is reasonable.
- Repeating an inadequate sample once and then moving to hysteroscopy is a common local approach.
- A focal mass on the scan warrants direct visualisation even when the biopsy is benign, since a blind sample can miss it (FIGO PALM-COEIN, Munro et al., 2018).
- Heavy bleeding with symptoms of volume loss needs same-day assessment.
The FIGO system classifies causes and doesn't dictate referral order, and I'm not aware of one national rule that fixes it; most pathways are local consensus.
❓ Which of those three triggers will the clinic nurses find hardest to apply consistently?

Writing the plan for the clinic nurses. Challenge it where it is weak:
- Pipelle and scan at the first visit
- Refer if the sample is inadequate twice, a focal mass is seen, or heavy bleeding comes with dizziness
- Hold aspirin until the bleeding settles
I'll check tranexamic acid dosing against our formulary first.

Weak spots I'd check:
- Pregnancy should be excluded before any sampling.
- Ask about easy bruising and family bleeding history, since coagulopathy is the C in the FIGO system (FIGO PALM-COEIN, Munro et al., 2018).
- Check haemoglobin, so anaemia isn't missed.
- Aspirin: agree the hold with whoever prescribed it, if it was for secondary prevention.
Checking tranexamic acid dosing against your formulary is the right habit; I can't see your local formulary.
❓ How will you tell, in a few months, whether the nurses apply the heavy-bleeding trigger the same way?

Summary for my notes: sample at the first visit, scan the same day, refer on a clean sample only if she keeps bleeding. Lining thickness doesn't gate her biopsy. Hyperplasia evidence in women with her BMI is thinner than I assumed, and repeat sampling stays. Monday: add a pregnancy test to the nurse checklist and audit our clinic biopsies for inadequate samples.

That summary matches what we discussed. Sampling her at the first visit and refusing to let lining thickness decide it is well supported for a woman with her risk factors (FIGO PALM-COEIN, Munro et al., 2018 classifies causes, and does not itself set that rule). Auditing your inadequate-sample rate is a sound way to find out how well the local pathway works.
❓ What inadequate-sample rate would make you change how the clinic takes the sample?
